title: Why Human Giants Defy the Laws of Physics
gist: Drawing on Galileo's 1638 argument in Dialogues Concerning Two New Sciences, the article explains that mythical human giants (Cyclops, folklore giants) are physically impossible at human proportions—a scaled-up body would collapse under its own weight without different anatomical proportions.

insights.claim: Galileo Galilei argued in his 1638 text Dialogues Concerning Two New Sciences that the folklore conception of giants—a humanlike creature simply scaled up in size while retaining normal human body proportions—is physically impossible.
insights.speaker: Joel David Hamkins
insights.so_what: Cites the historical origin of the square-cube law argument against naive biological scaling, a foundational physics concept with broader applications to engineering and biomechanics.
insights.quote: In his foundational 1638 text Dialogues Concerning Two New Sciences, Galileo Galilei argues that this folklore understanding of the nature of giants is fundamentally flawed. He contends that this idea of a massive humanlike creature is, quite simply, physically impossible.

insights.claim: Without different anatomical proportions than ordinary humans, a giant scaled up in the manner of mythological figures (Homer's Cyclops, Jack the Giant Killer's giants) would collapse under its own weight.
insights.speaker: Joel David Hamkins
insights.so_what: Frames the article's core physics thesis: scale invariance fails for load-bearing biological structures, a concept relevant to any discussion of biomechanical scaling limits.
insights.quote: Without different anatomical proportions, a scaled-up body would collapse under its own weight.
